package_info.package_name: sniperv1 (and related: sniperv2, snipersee, sniperser, deuplouded)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages execute a Windows info-stealer and crypto-stealer ('Bladeroid') immediately upon installation, exfiltrating sensitive browser, crypto wallet, and session data to an attacker-controlled domain. The packages use obfuscated/encrypted payloads, misleading documentation, and postinstall scripts to evade detection and maximize data theft.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Automatically executes index.js upon package installation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Postinstall scripts are commonly abused in npm malware to trigger malicious payloads as soon as the package is installed, without user interaction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages rarely require postinstall scripts unless performing necessary build or setup tasks. Here, the script is used solely to launch malware.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages use postinstall for compiling native modules or setup.
key_indicators: postinstall script with no legitimate build/setup purpose
triggers execution of further obfuscated code

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Loads and executes the next-stage payload (gayy.js), despite misleading comments and documentation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code contains misleading comments and references to non-existent files (sa.js), but actually loads an obfuscated payload (gayy.js). This is a common evasion tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not mislead about which files are executed, nor do they load obfuscated payloads without clear purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rare in legitimate packages; sometimes used in code splitting or dynamic imports, but not with misleading intent.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Decrypts and executes a large, obfuscated Node.js payload containing the actual info-stealer/crypto-stealer logic.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscation and encryption of payloads, with the decryption key hardcoded, is a classic anti-analysis and anti-signature tactic. The use of eval to execute decrypted code is highly suspicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not encrypt their own code and execute it at runtime, especially with hardcoded keys.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rare; sometimes used for licensing or DRM, but not for core package logic.
key_indicators: payload size much larger than visible code

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Searches for and collects sensitive data from browsers, crypto wallet extensions, and exfiltrates it to an attacker-controlled domain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing browser storage, cookies, and crypto wallet data is a hallmark of info-stealer malware. Exfiltration to a suspicious domain confirms malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not access or exfiltrate user browser or wallet data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate backup or migration tools may access browser data, but never exfiltrate it to untrusted domains.
key_indicators: enumeration of browser and wallet data paths

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Searches for and steals session tokens or files for popular social media, messaging, and FTP applications, enabling account hijacking.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Targeting session data for hijacking is a direct attack on user privacy and account security.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate package should access or exfiltrate session tokens for unrelated applications.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; session hijacking is always malicious.
key_indicators: enumeration of session/token files for unrelated apps

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Sends all collected sensitive data to a hardcoded attacker-controlled webhook endpoint.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating sensitive data to a suspicious domain is a clear indicator of malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not send user data to untrusted external servers.

attack_chain.action: Package is installed, triggering postinstall script.
index.js loads and executes obfuscated payload (gayy.js), despite misleading documentation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Decryption and execution of main malware payload

attack_chain.action: gayy.js decrypts and evals the main info-stealer/crypto-stealer code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious data collection routines

attack_chain.action: Malware searches for and collects sensitive browser, crypto wallet, and session data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Preparation of stolen data for exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Exfiltrates all stolen data to attacker-controlled webhook endpoint.

behavioral_signatures: npm package with postinstall script executing index.js or similar entrypoint
Dynamic loading and execution of obfuscated/encrypted JavaScript payloads
Access to browser, crypto wallet, and session data directories
Network exfiltration to hardcoded, suspicious domains
file_indicators: Presence of index.js and gayy.js (or similarly named files) in npm package
Obfuscated/encrypted payloads in secondary JS files
References to non-existent files (e.g., sa.js) in comments or documentation
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP POST requests to bladeroid.xyz or bladeroid.com
Unusual traffic to domains registered with Turkticaret or with Turkish-language error messages
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for postinstall scripts that execute JavaScript files. Flag packages that load and eval obfuscated or encrypted code, especially if the decryption key is hardcoded. Detect access to browser, crypto wallet, and session data directories by Node.js processes spawned from npm scripts. Alert on outbound network connections to known malicious domains such as bladeroid.xyz. Use static analysis to identify misleading documentation or comments referencing non-existent files.
